A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

content.name: ask

questions.question: Should we key the POST /orders rate limit on `x-customer-id` only, rather than client IP or both?

options.label: x-customer-id only
options.tradeoff: Correctly attributes both abuse and legitimate bursts to the paying account; assumes the header is always present (which src/server.ts already enforces).
options.description: Use the existing required `x-customer-id` header as the rate-limit key.

options.label: client IP only
options.tradeoff: Simple to implement but breaks behind NAT/shared egress and lets a customer bypass by adding IPs.
options.description: Rate-limit by `req.headers.get('x-forwarded-for')` or socket remoteAddress.

options.label: both, with separate limits
options.tradeoff: Most precise but more state, harder to explain, and unnecessary if every request already carries x-customer-id.
options.description: Maintain two counters per customer and per IP.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 14 lists three keying options. src/server.ts line 7 already requires `x-customer-id` and returns 401 if it is missing.
brief.what: The key determines which identity is throttled. The incident was one customer id creating 40,000 orders, and enterprise limits must attach to the account, not an IP.
brief.how: This decides middleware lookup logic and whether enterprise overrides are per-customer or per-IP-range.

evidence.note: Lists keying options but does not decide.

questions.question: Should we use a token bucket algorithm instead of fixed or sliding window?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Allows legitimate bursts up to a bucket size while capping average rate; fewer Redis operations than sliding window.
options.description: Bucket per customer; each request removes a token, tokens refill at a fixed rate.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothest enforcement but more Redis round-trips and more complex Lua/Redis logic.
options.description: Track each request timestamp and count requests in the current window.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest implementation but allows 2x spikes at window boundaries and can unfairly throttle legitimate bursts.
options.description: Count requests in the current time bucket (e.g., current minute).

brief.where: PLAN.md line 15 lists three algorithms. About 20 enterprise customers legitimately burst.
brief.what: The algorithm determines how strictly the limit is enforced and how customers experience throttling.
brief.how: This decides the Redis data structure, the Lua script (if any), and the shape of the limit configuration.

evidence.note: Enterprise burst behavior makes algorithm choice important.

questions.question: Should the rate-limit counters live in the Redis cluster rather than in each instance's memory?

options.label: Redis cluster

questions.question: Should we key the POST /orders rate limit on `x-customer-id` only, rather than client IP or both?

options.label: x-customer-id only
options.tradeoff: Correctly attributes both abuse and legitimate bursts to the paying account; assumes the header is always present (which src/server.ts already enforces).
options.description: Use the existing required `x-customer-id` header as the rate-limit key.

options.label: client IP only
options.tradeoff: Simple to implement but breaks behind NAT/shared egress and lets a customer bypass by adding IPs.
options.description: Rate-limit by `req.headers.get('x-forwarded-for')` or socket remoteAddress.

options.label: both, with separate limits
options.tradeoff: Most precise but more state, harder to explain, and unnecessary if every request already carries x-customer-id.
options.description: Maintain two counters per customer and per IP.

brief.how: This decides middleware lookup logic and whether enterprise overrides are per-customer or per-IP-range.

questions.question: Should we use a token bucket algorithm instead of fixed or sliding window?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Allows legitimate bursts up to a bucket size while capping average rate; fewer Redis operations than sliding window.
options.description: Bucket per customer; each request removes a token, tokens refill at a fixed rate.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothest enforcement but more Redis round-trips and more complex Lua/Redis logic.
options.description: Track each request timestamp and count requests in the current window.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest implementation but allows 2x spikes at window boundaries and can unfairly throttle legitimate bursts.
options.description: Count requests in the current time bucket (e.g., current minute).
